extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of constitutional law and political science (those studying the American federal system)
extracted.subtask_description: Explanatory textbook material setting out the principles, limits, and working relations of the U.S. national and state governments, with historical examples and judicial grounding. It describes what powers each level has, how conflicts are resolved, and practical rules for citizens and officials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and meeting of presidential electors
rubrics_metrics.description: It requires similarly that presidential electors be chosen, meet, and vote in the States, and that their votes be transmitted to the national capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States determine the manner of choosing electors (historically legislatures sometimes chose; now popular vote). Explains procedural requirement that electors meet and vote within States and that votes be sent to national capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: State duty to organize and arm militia
rubrics_metrics.description: It requires each State to organize and arm its militia, which, when duly summoned for active service, are placed under the command of the President.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States must maintain militia forces; when federally summoned for active service those forces fall under presidential command — shows one area of obligatory state action supporting national defence.

rubrics_metrics.name: States must maintain a republican form of government
rubrics_metrics.description: It requires each State to maintain a republican form of government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutionally guaranteed; conversely, the national government may be required to protect a State against invasion or domestic violence to secure that republican form (President must notify Congress if a State departs from it).

rubrics_metrics.name: National government does not compel state financial support or administrative subordination
rubrics_metrics.description: The National government does not call upon the States, as commonwealths, to contribute funds to its support; issue administrative orders to the States (except as needed to secure a republican form); or require the States to submit their laws to it or veto such as it disapproves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that national finance and direct enforcement by federal officers make such compulsion unnecessary; contrasts with other federations where central government may demand contributions or issue directives to state administrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supremacy of federal law over conflicting state law (Art. VI §2)
rubrics_metrics.description: State laws are ipso jure invalid if they conflict with the Constitution or any treaty or law duly made under it (Art. vi. § 2); while if they do not so conflict they are valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives the Supremacy Clause rule: conflicting state acts are null. Explains practical implication: Congress or treaties can displace state law; examples and citations to cases illustrate application.

rubrics_metrics.name: National government independence from state action
rubrics_metrics.description: The National government does not allow its structure to be dependent on the action of the States; designed to make it impossible for a State or group of States to jeopardize by inaction or hostile action the existence of the central government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical illustration: despite de facto secession of eleven States in 1860–61, federal institutions (e.g., Congress, presidential elections) continued to operate legally. Emphasizes design intent to keep central government operative regardless of some States' conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of authority within respective spheres
rubrics_metrics.description: A State is, within its proper sphere, just as legally supreme, just as well entitled to give effect to its own will, as is the National government within its sphere; both hold by a like title, all authority flows from the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the dual-sovereignty conception: neither level may trespass on the other's domain; bad motives of a State do not justify federal interference unless the State infringes federal authority. Notes judicial role in adjudicating disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: No express constitutional grant to coerce rebellious State; secession not mentioned
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no grant of power to the National government to coerce a recalcitrant or rebellious State. Another is that nothing is said as to the right of secession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that framers omitted explicit provisions on coercion or secession as compromises; historical context (Civil War) resolved these knots, and modern judicial doctrine treats the Union as indestructible (Texas v. White cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Union treated as indestructible; national force to preserve it
rubrics_metrics.description: It is now admitted that the Union is not a mere compact...but an instrument of perpetual efficacy...It follows from the recognition of the indestructibility of the Union that there must somewhere exist a force capable of preserving it. The National government is now admitted to be such a force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justifies that the national government may exercise all powers essential to preserve and protect its own existence and that of the States; but warns about potential abuse and the political checks that limit it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checks on abuse of federal power (public opinion, amendment, revolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abuse [of federal powers] may be checked only when public opinion supports it; change can occur by constitutional amendment or, improbably, revolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains modes by which fundamental change may happen: lawful amendment process if majority wills it, or extralegal revolution; implies constitutional limits are ultimately upheld by political will.

rubrics_metrics.name: State role in forming national government (electors, senators, franchise)
rubrics_metrics.description: The States serve to form the National government by choosing presidential electors, by choosing senators, and by fixing the franchise which qualifies citizens to vote for members of the House of Representatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes practical latitude left to States (e.g., method of appointing electors, prescribing franchise for federal elections). Examples: some States allow aliens or women to vote in State elections thereby affecting federal elections; limitations include constitutional amendments (e.g., Fifteenth Amendment).

rubrics_metrics.name: State discretion in prescribing franchise for federal elections limited by constitutional amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: A State may, by its power of prescribing the franchise for its State elections, prescribe whatever franchise it pleases for the election of its members of the Federal House of Representatives...The only restriction imposed on State discretion in this respect is that of the fifteenth amendment, which forbids any person to be deprived of suffrage on account of race, colour, or previous condition of servitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives examples (aliens voting, women in some states historically) and notes federal constitutional limits that override discriminatory state provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific powers withheld from States by the Federal Constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Constitution deprives the States of certain powers they would otherwise enjoy. Some of these, such as that of making treaties, are obviously unpermissible...Others...seriously restrain their daily action (e.g., liability to be sued in Federal courts by another State or foreign power; cannot tax exports or imports except with consent of Congress; cannot pass laws impairing contract obligations; must surrender fugitives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists typical prohibitions and practical consequences; these are judicially enforceable restrictions with federal courts as referees.

rubrics_metrics.name: State acts violating constitutional restrictions are null and void
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether they have transgressed any of these restrictions is a question for the courts of law, and, if ... decided that they have transgressed, their act, be it legislative or executive, is null and void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains judicial review role; cites that state statutes conflicting with Constitution are invalidated by courts; gives context that many state statutes historically violated commerce provisions and are struck down.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional legislation prevails over conflicting State statutes; field of concurrent legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: When an Act of Congress, made within the powers conferred by the Constitution, conflicts with a State statute, the former prevails against the latter...The field of this so-called concurrent legislation is large, for Congress has not yet exercised all the powers vested in it of superseding State action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: bankruptcy laws previously passed by Congress, then repealed (leaving state law), later re-enacted (replacing state statutes). Explains effect: a valid federal law displaces prior state law to extent of conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumptions when assigning legislative power (favor states; require grant for Congress)
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining the powers of Congress on the one hand and of a State government on the other, opposite methods have to be followed. The presumption is always in favour of the State; and in order to show that it cannot legislate on a subject, there must be pointed out within the four corners of the Constitution some express prohibition...On the other hand, the presumption is always against Congress, and to show that it can legislate, some positive grant of power to Congress in the Constitution must be pointed out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes exceptions: powers may be implied (incidental/instrumental) — necessary implication (McCulloch v. Maryland cited). Helps interpret scope of federal vs state competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congress empowered (and sometimes constrained) to enforce constitutional amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: As regards amendments passed for the protection of the lately liberated negroes...they interdict the States from...Congress is also empowered, which practically means enjoined, to 'enforce by appropriate legislation' the prohibitions laid upon the States. Congress has done so, but some of its efforts have been held to go beyond the directions of the amendments, and to be therefore void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that while Congress may pass enforcement legislation, courts may invalidate acts that exceed the scope of the enforcement clause; gives balance between legislative action and judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential modes of interfering with States
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the President interferes with a State, he does so either under his duty to give effect to the legislation of Congress, or under the discretionary executive functions which the Constitution has entrusted to him...If an insurrection broke out against the authority of the Union, he would...send Federal troops to suppress it. If there should be rival State governments...the President might...recognize and support the one which he deemed regular and constitutional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives concrete duties and discretionary authorities: reporting to Congress when State departs from republican form, suppressing insurrections, recognizing governments in disputed cases (historical examples like post-Civil War interventions cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal criminal jurisdiction and enforcement powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Offences against Federal statutes are justiciable in Federal courts, and punishable under Federal authority. There is no Federal common law of crimes. Resistance offered to the enforcement of a Federal statute may be suppressed by Federal authority. Attacks on the property of the Federal government may be repelled, and disturbances thence arising may be quelled by Federal authority. The judgments pronounced in civil causes by Federal courts are executed by the officers of these courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarizes the categories of federal enforcement: federal statutory offenses, protection of federal property and operations, execution of federal judgments. Emphasizes absence of a general federal common-law criminal code and the federal government's ability to use force in enforcement contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal aid to states for serious disturbances (presidential duty on application)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is bound on the application of the State legislature or executive to quell such disturbances by the armed forces of the Union, or by directing the militia of another State to enter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: Washington and the Whiskey Rebellion (1794), federal interventions after the Civil War, President Hayes during 1877 railway strikes, President Cleveland sending troops in 1894 to secure mail trains. Also notes states should suppress insurrections if they can and seek federal aid only in extreme cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual citizenship allegiance and conflict rule for citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: They [citizens] are citizens of the Union as well as of these States, and owe allegiance to both powers...Within the limits of its power, [federal authority] is higher than that of the State, and must be obeyed even at the risk of disobeying the State...Ascertain whether the Federal law is constitutional (i.e. such as Congress has power to pass). If it is, conform your conduct to it at all hazards. If it is not, disregard it, and obey the law of your State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a practical safe rule for private citizens faced with conflicting commands: obey constitutional federal law; otherwise obey state law. Example: Ho Ah Kow case where a state ordinance violated Fourteenth Amendment and was declared invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict between national and state executive officers
rubrics_metrics.description: If the national officer is acting within his constitutional powers, he is entitled to be obeyed in preference to a State official, and conversely, if the State official is within his powers, and the national officer acting in excess of those which the Federal Constitution confers, the State official is to be obeyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains operational rule for officials: obedience depends on whether action falls within constitutional powers; no blanket supremacy of one officer over another outside constitutional competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and practical operation of judicial power (venue, removal, and deference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every citizen can sue and be sued ... both in the courts of his State and in the Federal courts, but in some classes of cases the former, in others the latter, is the proper tribunal, while in many it is left to the choice of the parties...Suits are thus constantly transferred from State courts to Federal courts, but no one can ever reverse the process...Within its proper sphere of pure State law...there is no appeal from a State court to a Federal court...A Federal court in administering State law ought to reverse its own previous decision rather than depart from the view which the highest State court has taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains removal and appeal rules, the practical convenience of state courts (more numerous), reasons plaintiffs may prefer federal courts (independence, wider jury pool), and the complex interplay of state and federal jurisprudence with examples and normative guidance for which tribunal is appropriate.
